title: Repeated DNA Blocks

concept.title: Two sets: seen once, seen more than once
body: To find blocks of a fixed length that occur **more than once**, slide over the string and look at every block of that length. Keep a set `seen` of the blocks met so far. When a block is already in `seen`, it is a repeat, and you put it into a second set `repeated` (a set, so that a block found three times is still reported once).
The blocks may overlap each other. Strings can be put into hash sets just like numbers; the cost of hashing one block is its length (10 here), so the scan is O(n * 10).

statement: A DNA word consists of the letters A, C, G and T. Find all blocks of exactly 10 consecutive letters that occur more than once in the word (blocks may overlap). Print how many different such blocks there are, and then the blocks in alphabetical order, separated by spaces.
inputFormat: A single word of the letters A, C, G, T.
outputFormat: The first line: the number of repeated blocks.
The second line: the blocks in alphabetical order (an empty line if there are none).

examples.note: AAAAACCCCC and CCCCCAAAAA each occur twice.

hints: Look at every block of 10 letters.
Remember the blocks you have met in a set.
A block that is already in the set goes into a second set of repeated blocks; sort it at the end.

explanation: One set remembers the blocks seen so far; a block that is already in it is a repeat and goes into a second, sorted set.
solution.complexity: Time O(10 * n) on average, space O(10 * n).

code.python:
s = input().strip()

seen = set()
repeated = set()
for i in range(len(s) - 9):
    block = s[i:i + 10]
    if block in seen:
        repeated.add(block)
    else:
        seen.add(block)
result = sorted(repeated)
print(len(result))
print(*result)
